relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: The woman who once received her son back is warned to move before famine arrives.
She becomes a migrant with her household for seven years.
On return, she goes directly to power to reclaim house and field.
The king happens to be hearing stories about Elisha.
Her own living testimony walks into the room while her story is being told.
Restoration includes not only property but the produce lost during displacement.
The scene turns from restitution to a sick king in Damascus.
Hazael carries royal gifts and a question about recovery.
Forty camel-loads surround a single vulnerable question.
The answer separates illness from the death another human will cause.
Elisha sees what is coming and weeps before speaking it.
The future king is named through burned strongholds and violence against bodies least able to defend themselves.
Hazael recoils from the image of what he may become.
He returns and reports only the promise of recovery.
The next day, succession arrives through suffocation.
Judah's royal chronology continues inside Israel's dynastic shadow.
Jehoram's eight years begin at thirty-two.
Marriage connects houses, but responsibility remains personal.
The Davidic lamp restrains total destruction in the narrator's theology.
Edom breaks Judah's imperial hold and establishes its own king.
Night battle fails to restore stable control.
Edom and Libnah remain outside Judah's hand.
The royal record closes what the chapter does not narrate.
Jehoram dies and Ahaziah succeeds.
Another synchronized reign begins.
Athaliah's lineage enters the record without becoming an excuse to blame women for dynastic violence.
Ahaziah continues the policies of Ahab's house.
Alliance brings him into war against Hazael.
One wounded king returns to Jezreel, and another comes to see him.

contemplative_note: The chapter sets two kinds of power beside each other. One ruler restores a displaced woman's land and lost produce; another future ruler suffocates his king and will devastate families. Prophetic sight is shown not as thrill or superiority but as grief before preventable human cruelty.
